It means the most important safety feature in any car is the person holding the wheel. In this lesson you will learn the standard crash-prevention formula, why your mood matters before you even start the engine, why crawling along slower than traffic is not automatically safe, and how aggressive driving and road rage look from the driver's seat. Being alert means watching the whole scene around you, not just the bumper ahead. Being prepared means you have already thought about what other drivers might do, because the manual says never assume other drivers will not make mistakes. Acting in time means responding early and calmly. Expect the unexpected, and avoid panic, since a panicked move can turn a close call into something worse. A heated phone call or an argument at home can ride along with you if you let it. Second, think about your speed compared with everyone else. Some people assume that driving slower than other vehicles is always safer, but the manual says keeping up with the flow of traffic helps keep the road safe for everyone. That word progression matters, because it often starts small and builds. The acts include sudden changes of speed, improper or erratic lane changes, ignoring traffic control devices, failing to yield and following too closely. One everyday example of ignoring traffic control devices is the rolling right turn on red. A right turn on red still requires a full stop and yielding to traffic and pedestrians, and an incomplete stop counts among the dangers of ignoring traffic control devices. If you catch yourself doing any of these, it is time to reset.","fact_ids":["sec08-F03","sec08-R08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec08-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Aggressive driving versus road rage","fact_ids":["sec08-R09","sec08-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Aggressive driving: a chain of unlawful acts.","fact_ids":["sec08-R09","sec08-F03"]},{"text":"Road rage: a lost temper over traffic.","fact_ids":["sec08-R09","sec08-F03"]},{"text":"Signs: weaving, gestures, honking, flashing high beams.","fact_ids":["sec08-R09","sec08-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a distinction that trips people up. It shows up as running stop signs and red lights, speeding, tailgating, weaving, illegal passing on the right, gestures, screaming, honking or flashing high beams. Notice the overlap, since tailgating and speeding appear in both. The difference is the lost temper. A question about anger over a traffic incident points to road rage, while a list of unlawful habits points to aggressive driving.","fact_ids":["sec08-R09","sec08-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec08-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Spot the road rage","fact_ids":["sec08-R09","sec08-R06","sec08-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Weaving, honking, flashing high beams.","fact_ids":["sec08-R09","sec08-R06","sec08-F04"]},{"text":"What is it, and what do you do?","fact_ids":["sec08-R09","sec08-R06","sec08-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you merge onto a highway, and the driver behind you starts weaving, honking and flashing high beams at you. Which of the four types of distraction is this?","fact_ids":["sec08-F06"]},"answer":{"text":"Cognitive distraction, the mind off driving.","fact_ids":["sec08-F06"]},"rationale":{"text":"The four types are visual, manual, cognitive and auditory, and cognitive means the mind is off driving even when eyes and hands stay put.","fact_ids":["sec08-F06"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec08-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Attention keeps you alive","fact_ids":["sec08-F07","sec08-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Distraction and fatigue steal attention.","fact_ids":["sec08-F07","sec08-F09"]},{"text":"Both raise crash risk.","fact_ids":["sec08-F07","sec08-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson is about attention, the resource every other driving skill depends on. Two things steal it: distraction and fatigue. The New Jersey manual says distractions are one of the leading causes of crashes for teen drivers, and that a tired driver can be as dangerous as a drunk driver. Over the next few slides you will learn the four types of distraction, the most common distractions inside the car, why the safest phone call happens at the roadside, what Maggie's Law says about drowsy driving, how highway hypnosis creeps in, and which drivers are most at risk of falling asleep at the wheel.","fact_ids":["sec08-F07","sec08-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec08-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Four types of distraction","fact_ids":["sec08-F06","sec08-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Visual: eyes off the road.","fact_ids":["sec08-F06","sec08-F07"]},{"text":"Manual: hands off the wheel.","fact_ids":["sec08-F06","sec08-F07"]},{"text":"Cognitive: mind off driving.","fact_ids":["sec08-F06","sec08-F07"]},{"text":"Auditory: sounds that pull attention.","fact_ids":["sec08-F06","sec08-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"The manual sorts driving distraction into four types. Visual distraction takes your eyes off the road. Manual distraction takes your hands off the wheel. Cognitive distraction takes your mind off driving, even if your eyes and hands look busy with the job. Auditory distraction comes from sounds that pull your attention away. Many distractions mix several types at once. The stakes are real: a few seconds of inattention at highway speed can cover the length of a football field. That is a long stretch of road to cross with nobody really driving, and it is why distractions rank among the leading causes of crashes for teens.","fact_ids":["sec08-F06","sec08-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec08-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Common distractions and phones","fact_ids":["sec08-F08","sec08-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Texting, videos, GPS, music, photos.","fact_ids":["sec08-F08","sec08-F05"]},{"text":"Food, passengers, reaching, smart watches.","fact_ids":["sec08-F08","sec08-F05"]},{"text":"Even hands-free phones distract.","fact_ids":["sec08-F08","sec08-F05"]},{"text":"Stop at the roadside, then call.","fact_ids":["sec08-F08","sec08-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the manual's list of common distractions. Texting, scrolling or watching videos, and using a phone, even hands-free. Programming a GPS while moving, picking music and taking photos. Eating or drinking, turning to talk to passengers, reaching for items and using smart watches. Notice that hands-free phone use is on the list, so a free hand does not mean a free mind. New Jersey's handheld phone law has emergency exceptions, but the manual is clear that even then the safest choice is to stop at the roadside first and only then place a call. Set up your music and route before you roll.","fact_ids":["sec08-F08","sec08-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec08-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Fatigue and Maggie's Law","fact_ids":["sec08-F09","sec08-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Tired drivers react more slowly.","fact_ids":["sec08-F09","sec08-F10"]},{"text":"As dangerous as a drunk driver.","fact_ids":["sec08-F09","sec08-F10"]},{"text":"Maggie's Law covers knowingly driving sleep impaired.","fact_ids":["sec08-F09","sec08-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Fatigue does several things at once. A tired driver reacts more slowly, gets upset more easily, may fall asleep at the wheel, and can be as dangerous as a drunk driver. New Jersey takes this seriously in law. Maggie's Law, enacted in June two thousand three, makes it illegal to knowingly drive while impaired by lack of sleep. It also treats fatigued driving as recklessness under the vehicular homicide statute. The key word is knowingly: if you know you are too tired to drive safely and you drive anyway, the law treats that choice as reckless, not as an unlucky accident.","fact_ids":["sec08-F09","sec08-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec08-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Highway hypnosis on long drives","fact_ids":["sec08-F11","sec08-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"A trance after long periods at the wheel.","fact_ids":["sec08-F11","sec08-F12"]},{"text":"Never fix your eyes on one thing.","fact_ids":["sec08-F11","sec08-F12"]},{"text":"Rest every two hours or share driving.","fact_ids":["sec08-F11","sec08-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap that does not feel like danger while it is happening. Highway hypnosis is a trance-like state that sets in after long periods at the wheel. You may still be holding your lane, but your attention has drifted away. The manual's fix is simple: never fix your eyes on one thing for more than a few seconds. Keep scanning mirrors, gauges and the road far ahead. For long trips, plan breaks before you need them. The manual says rest every two hours, or share the driving with another licensed driver. Waiting until you feel sleepy means waiting too long.","fact_ids":["sec08-F11","sec08-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec08-u02-s6","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Who is most at risk","fact_ids":["sec08-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Sleep-deprived and solo drivers.","fact_ids":["sec08-F13"]},{"text":"Long trips and long rural roads.","fact_ids":["sec08-F13"]},{"text":"Young people, shift and commercial drivers.","fact_ids":["sec08-F13"]},{"text":"Sleep-inducing medicine or alcohol.","fact_ids":["sec08-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"The manual names the people most at risk of drowsy driving. Sleep-deprived people top the list. So do drivers on long trips without breaks, and drivers who are behind the wheel when they would normally be asleep. People on sleep-inducing medicine or alcohol are at risk, as are solo drivers with nobody to talk to or trade off with. Drivers on long rural roads are on the list too. Young people, shift workers and commercial drivers round out the list. If you fit one of these groups, build in rest stops, share the driving, and be honest with yourself about how tired you are.","fact_ids":["sec08-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec08-u02-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Name that distraction","fact_ids":["sec08-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Hands on the wheel, mind elsewhere.","fact_ids":["sec08-F06"]},{"text":"Which type is it?","fact_ids":["sec08-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: Dana keeps both hands on the wheel and her eyes pointed at the road, but her mind drifts to a problem at work. Fatigue slows your reactions and can make you as dangerous as a drunk driver, and Maggie's Law makes knowingly driving while impaired by lack of sleep illegal. What tells you it is time to move back to the right lane?","fact_ids":["sec08-F24"]},"answer":{"text":"Being well ahead, with the passed car visible in your rearview mirror.","fact_ids":["sec08-F24"]},"rationale":{"text":"The manual says return only when well ahead of the passed vehicle, and seeing it in your rearview mirror is a good sign; then cancel the signal.","fact_ids":["sec08-F24"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec08-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Talking without words","fact_ids":["sec08-F14","sec08-F23"]},"lines":[{"text":"Signals and eye contact share your plan.","fact_ids":["sec08-F14","sec08-F23"]},{"text":"Lane changes and passes need care.","fact_ids":["sec08-F14","sec08-F23"]}],"narration":{"text":"Driving is a constant conversation, even though nobody says a word. Then we move into lane changes and passing, which are some of the moments when drivers most need to read each other clearly. You will learn the safe lane-change routine, when passing is allowed at all, how to tell when it is safe to move back after a pass, and what to do when you are the one being passed.","fact_ids":["sec08-F14","sec08-F23"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec08-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"How drivers communicate","fact_ids":["sec08-F14","sec08-R11","sec08-R12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Turn or hand signals, eye contact.","fact_ids":["sec08-F14","sec08-R11","sec08-R12"]},{"text":"A tap of the horn when needed.","fact_ids":["sec08-F14","sec08-R11","sec08-R12"]},{"text":"At night, a quick low-high-low switch.","fact_ids":["sec08-F14","sec08-R11","sec08-R12"]},{"text":"Stay in the lane for your turn.","fact_ids":["sec08-F14","sec08-R11","sec08-R12"]}],"narration":{"text":"The manual lists several ways to communicate with other drivers. Use turn signals or hand signals, make eye contact, give a tap of the horn when needed, and at night use a quick switch from low beams to high and back. Your lane position talks too: always stay in the lane that shows the direction you intend to turn, so others are not surprised. In town or city traffic, be patient and avoid quick turns or lane changes. If you ever must pull off the road, switch on the emergency flashers so everyone around you knows your car is not moving with traffic.","fact_ids":["sec08-F14","sec08-R11","sec08-R12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec08-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Safe lane changes","fact_ids":["sec08-F23","sec08-R17"]},"lines":[{"text":"Check the rearview mirror.","fact_ids":["sec08-F23","sec08-R17"]},{"text":"Glance back at the blind spot.","fact_ids":["sec08-F23","sec08-R17"]},{"text":"Always signal; never straddle.","fact_ids":["sec08-F23","sec08-R17"]},{"text":"Change lanes only when necessary.","fact_ids":["sec08-F23","sec08-R17"]}],"narration":{"text":"A lane change has a simple routine. Check the rearview mirror, glance back at the blind spot, and always signal. While you do this, never straddle a lane, because riding between lanes leaves other drivers guessing which one you want. Before you even start the routine, ask whether the move is needed. The manual says pass or change lanes only when necessary, only if it can be done without speeding, and only where signs and pavement markings allow it. If a pass would require you to speed, or the markings say no, the safe answer is to stay where you are and wait.","fact_ids":["sec08-F23","sec08-R17"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec08-u03-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Passing versus being passed","fact_ids":["sec08-F24","sec08-F25"]},"lines":[{"text":"Passing: return when it shows in your mirror.","fact_ids":["sec08-F24","sec08-F25"]},{"text":"Signal, return, then cancel the signal.","fact_ids":["sec08-F24","sec08-F25"]},{"text":"Being passed: stay in lane and slow down.","fact_ids":["sec08-F24","sec08-F25"]}],"narration":{"text":"Two situations sound alike but call for opposite moves.
